newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bankers say Pakistan debt scheme could backfire.
newsitem.headline: Bankers say Pakistan debt scheme could backfire.

text.p: Pakistanis have responded warmly to Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's appeal for funds to help shrink the $30 billion foreign debt, but bankers and economists said on Wednesday the scheme could backfire.
The chief economist of a foreign bank, speaking anonymously, said the plan might ease Pakistan's immediate foreign exchange crunch but could store up trouble for the future.
"It has been launched on the assumption that Pakistan will be able to correct the imbalances of its external sector and will have enough cash in reserves in the next two years.
"But it is a dangerous gamble. If that does not happen, and Pakistan continues to have a large current account deficit and the situation deteriorates, people may react angrily," he said.
"This may result in a political crisis and in turn exacerbate the economic crisis," he said.
Sharif, convincing winner of the February 3 elections, has vowed to "break the begging-bowl" and reduce Pakistan's reliance on foreign borrowing to finance its current account deficit.
In a televised speech last week, he appealed for help from Pakistanis both at home and abroad.

Contributors can make donations, give an interest-free loan of at least US$1,000 repayable in two to five years, or place a minimum of $1,000 in an interest-bearing, fixed-term deposit maturing in two to five years with profits payable quarterly.

"I would not be surprised if a total of $1 billion is deposited in the scheme in view of the attractive returns offered," the chief economist said. "But high returns do not necessarily result in huge deposits."
The returns offered range from 7.5 percent a year on two-year dollar deposits to nine percent on five-year deposits.

The economist said the State (central) Bank of Pakistan had lured only $450 million in institutional deposits when it offered a 17 percent return on the rupee equivalent of foreign exchange deposits under a special scheme launched in October.
Bankers said that scheme had an estimated return in dollar terms of around 12 percent a year.

The chief analyst at a foreign investment bank said Sharif's idea might stretch the maturity of foreign exchange deposits estimated at $9 billion if savers shift their funds from three- to six-month deposits into the two-year special account.

"This can be a dangerous gamble as it actually does not mean fresh money is coming in. On the other hand, the government will have to be prepared for a massive withdrawal when the deposits start maturing two years down the line," he said.
He said few people were likely to put money into deposits with longer maturities than the two-year minimum.
"The danger is that the whole exercise may prove to be a breather only, and may only delay a forex crunch which may turn out to be a much larger crisis," the banker said.
Sharif, during his first stint in power, allowed individuals to open foreign exchange deposits in 1991 to boost reserves then at around $400 million and to meet a payments crisis, he noted.

"It paid off initially as the government used part of it for beefing up reserves and financing the current account deficit, but now the financial sector of Pakistan has a liability of $9 billion against these deposits," he said.
An economic bulletin of ABN AMRO Bank N.V. said apart from short-term borrowing from the international market, Pakistan was increasingly using forex deposits to fund its external deficit.

"Since the deficit has risen sharply from $2.16 billion in 1994/95 to $4.24 billion in 1995/96, while long-term capital inflows actually fell, Pakistan had to resort to short-term borrowing and its foreign currency accounts to finance the external deficit," it said.
